summary: Describes the SURVEY program at MIT-DMCG that regularly tried connecting to hosts to record whether they were reachable and how fast they responded, and reports the results of its first months. It invites corrections to the data.

plainLanguage.summary: A program on one computer kept knocking on the door of every other computer every fifteen minutes to see who was home and how fast they answered. This note describes the program and shares its first results.

subtitle: The MIT-DMCG SURVEY program, which tried to reach every ARPANET host every 15 minutes to see who was answering.

tldr.problem: Users and implementers had no regular record of which ARPANET hosts were reachable, or how quickly they responded.
tldr.mechanism: A SURVEY program on the MIT-DMCG ITS PDP-10 tries a connection to the LOGGER (socket 1) of each listed host every 15 minutes, and records one of five statuses plus the response time.
tldr.outcome: The RFC reports the first months of data and admits the limits of the method, such as counting scheduled downtime against a host. The unit metadata lists RFC 530 as a later update.

today: The unit metadata lists RFC 530 as a later update to this report and gives its status as Unknown. The data is a snapshot from December 1971 to March 1972.

sections.title: The SURVEY Program
sections.content:
Several months before this March 1972 note, a SURVEY program was implemented on the MIT-DMCG ITS PDP-10 to gather information on the availability of hosts on the ARPANET. The RFC has three aims: to announce the service and how to reach it, to present the results of its first few months, and to have errors in the data or the collection methods corrected.

Whenever the MIT-DMCG ITS time-sharing system is in normal operation, a survey starts at 15-minute intervals. The program tries to establish a connection to the LOGGER (socket 1) of each host in its table, and records the result of each attempt. To cause the least processing at the surveyed hosts, it aborts the Initial Connection Protocol before reading the transmitted socket number. If the connection succeeds, the host's average request-for-connection response time, in seconds, is updated.
sections.plainLanguage: Every fifteen minutes the program rings each computer's doorbell to see if someone answers, and notes how long the answer took. It hangs up quickly so the other computer is barely disturbed.

sections.title: The Five Statuses and the Commands
sections.content:
Each test ends in one of five statuses: LOGGER available when the connection completes; LOGGER not responding when an RFC is sent and there is no response within 20 seconds; LOGGER rejecting when the NCP returns a CLOSE; NCP not responding when a RESET times out after 15 seconds; and HOST dead when the IMP returns a host-dead status.

To read the data, a user first follows the scenario in RFC 254 to reach NETWRK, the DMCG user Telnet. Seven commands relate to survey data, including SUMMARY.OF.SURVEYS, which summarizes the most recent information; HISTORY.OF., which gives a host's recent history; ACTIVE.HOSTS, which lists hosts that accepted a connection in the last 24 hours; and BEST.SURVEY. Long-term versions cover everything since December 13, 1971. Here, recent means within the last 24 hours or less.
sections.plainLanguage: Each knock ends in one of five results: answered, no answer, door closed, the whole house not listening, or nobody home at all. A user can read the notes through a set of simple commands.

sections.title: Results and Their Limits
sections.content:
The table covers 6528 surveys from 09:55:18 on 12/13/71 to 08:50:41 on 03/20/72, listing each host's percentage up and average response time. Examples include ucla-ccn at 070% and mit-dmcg at 093%, while several hosts show 000%. Here, up means that the LOGGER is accepting connections.

The authors name several shortcomings. The program can only run when the MIT-DMCG system and its IMP are operating, so the 94% figure for MIT-DMCG is inaccurate and should be closer to 66%. SURVEY runs on a 24-hour basis and does not consider advertised uptime, so MIT-DMCG will never be better than 67% on a Tuesday, when the machine is unavailable from 4 p.m. to midnight. And the Lincoln Lab TX-2 shows as never available because of an as yet undiagnosed problem under investigation.
sections.plainLanguage: The chart has known mistakes, and the report admits them. It cannot run when its own computer is down, and it counts planned closed hours as if the computers were broken.
